entries.root_cause: Persistence-call matching still admitted only a bounded number of grouping parentheses around receiver/member expressions, so an additional grouping layer preserved the same forbidden write while escaping structural recognition.
Persistence receiver alias discovery handled declaration initializers but not ordinary later assignments such as store = database, leaving post-declaration aliases outside the write fence.

Secret taint propagation only modeled simple identifier assignment and therefore lost raw credential provenance when object destructuring renamed a secret field before a response/log/persistence sink.
The PostgreSQL DDL object grammar remained finite and omitted TABLESPACE, allowing governed artifacts to create new storage authority even though G2 owns no persistence infrastructure.

Compound forbidden concepts were matched inside individual identifiers but not across route/string separators, so an excluded source-cutover endpoint could be encoded as source-cutover and pass scope.
Provider-native authority detection recognized direct dot/quoted computed properties but did not normalize statically concatenated computed member names such as provider["permi" + "ssions"].

The fail-closed non-ASCII/confusable fence covered governed artifact contents but not governed path text, allowing cross-script confusables in directory/file names to evade forbidden path-token matching.
Secret-flow detection treated secret vocabulary inside ordinary string literals as live tainted data, creating false positives for bounded validation messages such as password is required.

The authorization PR path allowlist and authorization workflow filters were not advanced with all governed adversarial-learning ledger fragments, so the exact reviewed HEAD could reject its own historical learning artifacts and ledger-only hardening could evade the dedicated authorization workflow trigger.
Persistence invocation hardening treated ordinary call, call and apply as equivalent but omitted JavaScript optional-call syntax, allowing the same forbidden write through member?.(...).
Raw-secret taint propagation modeled declaration initializers and destructuring but not ordinary later assignments, allowing a credential alias introduced after declaration to reach a sink untainted.
Secret sink-wrapper discovery recognized function declarations and parenthesized arrow parameters but omitted standard unparenthesized single-parameter arrows.
The PostgreSQL DDL grammar remained an enumerated object set and omitted SERVER, leaving foreign-data authority creation outside the no-G2-owned-DDL fence.

Provider-native authority detection was expression-scoped but tied to the literal provider receiver, so simple and transitive provider aliases could carry provider role/permission authority without detection.
Executable escape normalization decoded Unicode identifier escapes but not JavaScript hexadecimal string escapes, allowing forbidden route/capability text to be hidden behind \xNN sequences.

Static computed-member normalization accepted quoted concatenations but omitted JavaScript template literals without interpolation, allowing an equivalent forbidden persistence method name to evade the write fence.
String-literal false-positive suppression erased computed property keys before secret-reference analysis, allowing payload["password"] to lose live secret provenance at a response sink.
Secret destructuring taint covered declarations but not parenthesized post-declaration destructuring assignments, dropping raw credential provenance before a sink.
Provider-native authority detection propagated scalar provider aliases but did not preserve provider provenance when authority fields were extracted by object destructuring.
The PostgreSQL DDL grammar recognized ordinary triggers but omitted the distinct EVENT TRIGGER object class, leaving repository-wide DDL execution authority outside the G2 no-owned-persistence fence.

Executable normalization decoded Unicode and hexadecimal escapes but retained JavaScript backslash-line-terminator continuations, allowing forbidden route text to be split physically while evaluating contiguously.

Persistence method extraction covered declaration-time object destructuring but not parenthesized post-declaration destructuring assignments, allowing the same write method to be called through a late alias.
Computed secret-member analysis normalized direct literals but did not resolve statically known string aliases used as property keys, dropping raw-secret provenance at sinks.
Provider destructuring recognized ordinary source keys but compared computed key syntax literally, allowing authority fields extracted through static computed members and transitive provider aliases.
The no-G2-owned-DDL grammar still omitted PostgreSQL text-search object classes after prior multiword object hardening.

Forbidden-marker scanning decoded escapes and separators but did not fold statically concatenated string fragments, allowing a runtime route to differ from the source fragments inspected independently.
Secret-flow literal suppression handled single- and double-quoted strings but treated non-interpolated template text as executable secret data.
Static string folding accepted bare literals but not redundant balanced grouping around literal operands, allowing an equivalent forbidden route to evade reconstruction.
Static computed-member parsing split concatenation text without removing balanced grouping around member fragments, leaving equivalent secret, persistence and provider keys unresolved.
Secret sink recognition covered bare and dot-member calls but omitted static computed-member calls such as response bracket send.
Persistence invocation recognition modeled direct, optional and member apply calls but not Reflect.apply over a governed persistence method.
Provider alias propagation required an ungrouped provider expression immediately after assignment, so redundant grouping dropped provider provenance.
Destructured shorthand source parsing retained the default initializer as part of the source field name, hiding provider authority terms.
PostgreSQL DDL modifier coverage omitted RECURSIVE before VIEW, allowing a valid G2-owned recursive view through the reuse-only fence.
Provider-authority fallback treated provider and authority components anywhere in one identifier as related, so an intervening display component caused a false positive.
Reflect.apply recognition accepted only dot-member access to apply, so the statically equivalent computed Reflect bracket member bypassed persistence-write classification.
Computed secret-sink recognition required the member expression to remain ungrouped, so balanced parentheses erased an otherwise identical response-exposure path.
Provider-authority destructuring recognized grouped static keys but required an ungrouped provider source expression, dropping provider provenance before authorization use.
The PostgreSQL DDL grammar modeled shared modifiers but omitted object-specific modifier sequences before trigger, language and conversion object classes.
Provider-authority identifier fallback accepted a matching adjacent pair even when additional display-label components proved the identifier was not an authority flow.
Reflect apply normalization covered dot and computed member spelling but did not preserve the same call identity through balanced grouping around the callee.
Secret sink normalization accepted grouping around computed members but not around semantically equivalent ordinary dot-member sink expressions.
Raw-secret destructuring taint parsed renamed targets without removing default initializers, so valid target identifiers were discarded before propagation.
Static computed-key aliases were resolved only after an object receiver, leaving equivalent alias keys inside provider destructuring unnormalized.
PostgreSQL CREATE INDEX classification omitted the object-specific NULLS DISTINCT modifier sequence between UNIQUE and INDEX.
The hardened PostgreSQL object inventory extended CREATE detection but left ALTER and DROP delegated to the smaller core inventory, creating inconsistent authority coverage by verb.
Static alias discovery parsed the remainder of a variable statement as one initializer, so later top-level declarators invalidated otherwise static key aliases.
Raw-secret sink invocation modeled direct calls but not call and apply indirection over the same governed response member.
horizontal_audit: direct call and apply sink invocation

entries.root_cause: Secret taint propagation recognized ordinary assignment but omitted JavaScript logical assignment operators that can select the same secret operand.
Persistence invocation equivalence covered direct call call/apply and extracted aliases but omitted immediate invocation of a bound governed method.
The PostgreSQL ALTER and DROP inventory omitted remaining authority-bearing multiword forms for default privileges, large objects and owned objects.
Initial secret taint relied on identifier vocabulary even when a statically literal initializer established harmless display-message provenance.
Secret sink invocation equivalence covered direct call/apply but omitted immediate invocation of a bound response method.
Literal-backed taint exemption operated by identifier name across the artifact, suppressing a later raw-secret property occurrence with the same spelling.
Variable statement discovery stopped at nested semicolons and newlines without tracking balanced syntax, so later declarators and static aliases disappeared.
The PostgreSQL ALTER inventory omitted SYSTEM despite its authority to change database-wide server configuration.
Balanced declaration scanning treated every top-level newline as termination even when a trailing comma made continuation syntactically explicit.
Declaration boundary scanning interpreted delimiter characters inside JavaScript comments as executable statement structure.
Template literals were modeled as flat quotes, so nested templates inside interpolation corrupted statement-boundary tracking.
Reflect apply equivalence was enforced for persistence writes but not for raw-secret response sink invocation.
Bind invocation matching used a non-balanced argument fragment, losing the final call when the bound receiver expression contained parentheses.
Secret taint propagation omitted compound assignments that retain a tainted right-hand value in the target binding.
Literal-backed display provenance rejected template interpolation even when every interpolated expression was itself statically literal.
The PostgreSQL authority fence enumerated schema-object DDL but omitted privilege and ownership statement families.
Reflect.apply secret-sink recognition normalized only direct dot-member targets, allowing an equivalent statically computed response method to receive raw credential data.
Assignment taint parsing flattened newlines without first masking comments, so a multiline block comment truncated the right-hand secret expression before propagation.
The PostgreSQL authority fence classified object privileges and ownership transfer but did not treat role membership GRANT or ADMIN OPTION revocation as authority mutations.
Variable declaration discovery searched raw source text and could harvest declaration keywords inside comments as live static aliases.
Static template evaluation resolved only one interpolation layer, misclassifying nested all-literal interpolation as dynamic secret-bearing content.
Computed Reflect sink recognition allowed grouping around the whole member but not independently around its receiver, so an equivalent parenthesized receiver escaped the sink grammar.
Multiline-comment hardening flattened every source newline, erasing JavaScript automatic-semicolon-insertion boundaries and allowing unrelated following declarations to contaminate assignment taint.
PostgreSQL role-membership coverage matched bare GRANT and REVOKE vocabulary without SQL statement structure, turning ordinary UI text and application function names into false DDL findings.
horizontal_audit: ordinary display text and function names

entries.root_cause: Assignment taint used newline as an unconditional terminator and therefore truncated expressions whose continuation was structurally required inside balanced grouping.
Sink-call matching operated on raw source, so legal comments inside grouped receiver syntax interrupted an otherwise equivalent computed sink expression.
The PostgreSQL privilege inventory recognized TEMPORARY but omitted its valid TEMP alias.
Role-membership syntax remained textually indistinguishable from ordinary prose because matching was not restricted to SQL-bearing statements, bindings or execution calls.
